{{Short description|Number of orderings allowing ties}}
{{good article}}
[[Image:13-Weak-Orders.svg|thumb|The 13 possible strict weak orderings on a set of three elements {{math|1={''a'', ''b'', ''c''}}}]]
In [[number theory]] and [[enumerative combinatorics]], the '''ordered Bell numbers''' or '''Fubini numbers''' count the [[weak ordering]]s on a [[set (mathematics)|set]] of <math>n</math> elements. Weak orderings arrange their elements into a sequence allowing [[Tie (draw)|ties]], such as might arise as the outcome of a [[horse race]].{{r|horse|mendelson}}

The ordered Bell numbers were studied in the 19th century by [[Arthur Cayley]] and [[William Allen Whitworth]]. They are named after [[Eric Temple Bell]], who wrote about the [[Bell number]]s, which count the [[partition of a set|partitions of a set]]; the ordered Bell numbers count partitions that have been equipped with a [[total order]]. Their alternative name, the Fubini numbers, comes from a connection to [[Guido Fubini]] and [[Fubini's theorem]] on equivalent forms of multiple integrals. Because weak orderings have many names, ordered Bell numbers may also be called by those names, for instance as the numbers of preferential arrangements{{r|gross}} or the numbers of asymmetric generalized weak orders.{{r|oeis}}

These numbers may be computed via a summation formula involving [[binomial coefficient]]s, or by using a [[recurrence relation]]. They also count  combinatorial objects that have a [[Bijective proof|bijective correspondence]] to the weak orderings, such as the ordered [[multiplicative partition]]s of a [[squarefree]] number{{r|sklar}} or the faces of all dimensions of a [[permutohedron]].{{r|ziegler}}

==Definitions and examples==
Weak orderings arrange their elements into a sequence allowing [[Tie (draw)|ties]]. This possibility describes various real-world scenarios, including certain sporting contests such as [[horse race]]s.{{r|horse|mendelson}} A weak ordering can be formalized axiomatically by a [[partially ordered set]] for which [[incomparability]] is an [[equivalence relation]]. The [[equivalence class]]es of this relation partition the elements of the ordering into subsets of mutually tied elements, and these equivalence classes can then be linearly ordered by the weak ordering. Thus, a weak ordering can be described as an [[ordered partition]], a partition of its elements and a [[total order]] on the sets of the partition.{{r|luce}} For instance, the ordered partition {''a'',''b''},{''c''},{''d'',''e'',''f''} describes an ordered partition on six elements in which ''a'' and ''b'' are tied and both less than the other four elements, and ''c'' is less than ''d'', ''e'', and ''f'', which are all tied with each other.

The <math>n</math>th ordered Bell number, denoted here <math>a(n)</math>, gives the number of distinct weak orderings on <math>n</math> elements.{{r|pip}} For instance, there are three weak orderings on the two elements ''a'' and ''b'': they can be ordered with ''a'' before ''b'', with ''b'' before ''a'', or with both tied. The figure shows the 13 weak orderings on three elements.
 
Starting from <math>n=0</math>, the ordered Bell numbers <math>a(n)</math> are
{{bi|left=1.6|1, 1, 3, 13, 75, 541, 4683, 47293, 545835, 7087261, 102247563, ... {{OEIS|A000670}}.}}

When the elements to be ordered are unlabeled (only the number of elements in each tied set matters, not their identities) what remains is a [[Composition (combinatorics)|composition]] or ordered integer partition, a representation of <math>n</math> as an ordered sum of positive integers. For instance, the ordered partition {''a'',''b''},{''c''},{''d'',''e'',''f''} discussed above corresponds in this way to the composition 2 + 1 + 3. The number of compositions of <math>n</math> is exactly <math>2^{n-1}</math>. This is because a composition is determined by its set of [[partial sum]]s, which may be any subset of the integers from 1 to <math>n-1</math>.{{r|oeis}}

==History==
[[File:Cayley ordered Bell trees.svg|thumb|300px|13 plane trees with ordered leaves and equal-length root-leaf paths, with the gaps between adjacent leaves labeled by the height above the leaves of the nearest common ancestor. These labels induce a weak ordering on the gaps, showing that the trees of this type are counted by the ordered Bell numbers.]]
The ordered Bell numbers appear in the work of {{harvtxt|Cayley|1859}}, who used them to count certain [[Tree (graph theory)#Plane tree|plane trees]] with <math>n+1</math> totally ordered leaves. In the trees considered by Cayley, each root-to-leaf path has the same length, and the number of nodes at distance <math>i</math> from the root must be strictly smaller than the number of nodes at distance <math>i+1</math>, until reaching the leaves.{{r|cayley}} In such a tree, there are <math>n</math> pairs of adjacent leaves, that may be weakly ordered by the height of their [[lowest common ancestor]]; this weak ordering determines the tree. {{harvtxt|Mor|Fraenkel|1984}} call the trees of this type "Cayley trees", and they call the sequences that may be used to label their gaps (sequences of <math>n</math> positive integers that include at least one copy of each positive integer between one and the maximum value in the sequence) "Cayley permutations".{{r|morfra}}

{{harvtxt|Pippenger|2010}} traces the problem of counting weak orderings, which has the same sequence as its solution, to the work of {{harvtxt|Whitworth|1886}}.{{r|pip|whitworth}} These numbers were called Fubini numbers by Louis Comtet, because they count the different ways to rearrange the ordering of sums or integrals in [[Fubini's theorem]], which in turn is named after [[Guido Fubini]].{{r|comtet}} The [[Bell number]]s, named after [[Eric Temple Bell]], count the [[partition of a set|partitions of a set]], and the weak orderings that are counted by the ordered Bell numbers may be interpreted as a partition together with a [[total order]] on the sets in the partition.{{r|km05}}

The equivalence between counting Cayley trees and counting weak orderings was observed in 1970 by [[Donald Knuth]], using an early form of the [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences]] (OEIS). This became one of the first successful uses of the OEIS to discover equivalences between different counting problems.{{r|oeis}}

==Formulas==
===Summation===
Because weak orderings can be described as total orderings on the subsets of a partition, one can count weak orderings by counting total orderings and partitions, and combining the results appropriately. The [[Stirling numbers of the second kind]], denoted  <math>\{{\scriptstyle{n\atop k}}\}</math>, count the partitions of an <math>n</math>-element set into <math>k</math> nonempty subsets. A weak ordering may be obtained from such a partition by choosing one of <math>k!</math> total orderings of its subsets. Therefore, the ordered Bell numbers can be counted by summing over the possible numbers of subsets in a partition (the parameter <math>k</math>) and, for each value of <math>k</math>, multiplying the number of partitions <math>\{{\scriptstyle{n\atop k}}\}</math> by the number of total orderings <math>k!</math>. That is, as a [[summation]] formula (See [[Stirling transform]]):{{r|good|sprugnoli}}
<math display=block>
a(n) = \sum_{k=0}^n k! \left\{\begin{matrix} n \\ k \end{matrix}\right\}
</math>
By general results on summations involving Stirling numbers, it follows that the ordered Bell numbers are [[log-convex]], meaning that they obey the inequality <math>a(n-1)a(n+1)\ge a(n)^2</math> for all <math>n>0</math>.{{r|lw07}}

[[File:Permutohedron.svg|thumb|A three-dimensional [[truncated octahedron]], with its vertices labeled by their four-dimensional coordinates as a [[permutohedron]]]]
An alternative interpretation of the terms of this sum is that they count the features of each dimension in a [[permutohedron]] of dimension <math>n</math>, with the <math>k</math>th term counting the features of dimension <math>n-k</math>. A permutohedron is a [[convex polytope]], the [[convex hull]] of points whose coordinate vectors are the [[permutation]]s of the numbers from 1 to <math>n+1</math>. These vectors are defined in a space of dimension <math>n+1</math>, but they and their convex hull all lie in an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[affine subspace]]. For instance, the three-dimensional permutohedron is the [[truncated octahedron]], the convex hull of points whose coordinates are permutations of (1,2,3,4), in the three-dimensional subspace of points whose coordinate sum is 10. This polyhedron has one volume (<math>k=0</math>), 14 two-dimensional faces (<math>k=1</math>), 36 edges (<math>k=2</math>), and 24 vertices (<math>k=3</math>). The total number of these faces is 1 + 14 + 36 + 24 = 75, an ordered Bell number, corresponding to the summation formula above for <math>n=3</math>.{{r|A019538}}

By expanding each Stirling number in this formula into a sum of [[binomial coefficient]]s, the formula for the ordered Bell numbers may be expanded out into a double summation. The ordered Bell numbers may also be given by an [[infinite series]]:{{r|pip|km05}}
<math display=block>
a(n) = \sum_{k=0}^n \sum_{j=0}^k (-1)^{k-j} \binom{k}{j}j^n
     = \frac12\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{m^n}{2^{m}}.
</math>

Another summation formula expresses the ordered Bell numbers in terms of the [[Eulerian number]]s <math>\langle{\scriptstyle{n\atop k}}\rangle</math>, which count the permutations of <math>n</math> items in which <math>k</math> pairs of consecutive items are in increasing order:{{r|vc95}}
<math display=block>a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 2^k \left\langle\begin{matrix} n \\ k \end{matrix}\right\rangle=A_n(2),</math>
where <math>A_n</math> is the <math>n</math>th [[Eulerian number | Eulerian polynomial]]. One way to explain this summation formula involves a mapping from weak orderings on the numbers from 1 to <math>n</math> to [[permutation]]s, obtained by sorting each tied set into numerical order. Under this mapping, each permutation with <math>k</math> consecutive increasing pairs comes from <math>2^k</math> weak orderings, distinguished from each other by the subset of the consecutive increasing pairs that are tied in the weak ordering.{{r|vc95}}

===Generating function and approximation===
As with many other integer sequences, reinterpreting the sequence as the coefficients of a [[power series]] and working with the function that results from summing this series can provide useful information about the sequence. 
The fast growth of the ordered Bell numbers causes their [[ordinary generating function]] to diverge; instead the [[exponential generating  function]] is used. For the ordered Bell numbers, it is:{{r|pip|km05|sprugnoli|gsww}}
<math display=block>\sum_{n=0}^\infty a(n)\frac{x^n}{n!} = \frac{1}{2-e^x}.</math>
Here, the left hand side is just the definition of the exponential generating function and the right hand side is the function obtained from this summation.
The form of this function corresponds to the fact that the ordered Bell numbers are the numbers in the first column of the [[infinite matrix]] <math>(2I-P)^{-1}</math>. Here <math>I</math> is the [[identity matrix]] and <math>P</math> is an infinite matrix form of [[Pascal's triangle]]. Each row of <math>P</math> starts with the numbers in the same row of Pascal's triangle, and then continues with an infinite repeating sequence of zeros.{{r|lewis}}

Based on a [[contour integration]] of this generating function, the ordered Bell numbers can be expressed by the infinite sum{{r|bailey|sklar}}
<math display=block>a(n)=\frac{n!}{2}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}(\log 2+2\pi ik)^{-(n+1)},\qquad n\ge1.</math>
Here, <math>\log</math> stands for the [[natural logarithm]]. This leads to an approximation for the ordered Bell numbers, obtained by using only the term for <math>k=0</math> in this sum and discarding the remaining terms:{{r|bailey|gross|sklar|sprugnoli|barthelemy}}
<math display=block>a(n)\sim \frac12 {n!}\,c^{n+1},</math>
where <math>c=\tfrac{1}{\log 2}\approx 1.4427</math>. Thus, the ordered Bell numbers are larger than the factorials by an exponential factor. Here, as in [[Stirling's approximation]] to the factorial, the <math>\sim</math> indicates [[asymptotic equivalence]]. That is, the ratio between the ordered Bell numbers and their approximation tends to one in the limit as <math>n</math> grows arbitrarily large. As expressed in [[little o notation]], the [[relative error]] is  <math>1\pm o(1)</math>, and the <math>o(1)</math> error term [[decays exponentially]] as <math>n</math> grows.{{r|sklar}}

Comparing the approximations for <math>a(n-1)</math> and <math>a(n)</math> shows that
<math display=block>
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{n\,a(n-1)}{a(n)}=\log 2.
</math>
For example, taking <math>n=5</math> gives the approximation <math>375/541\approx 0.693161</math> to <math>\log 2\approx 0.693145</math>.
This sequence of approximations, and this example from it, were calculated by [[Ramanujan]], using a general method for solving equations numerically (here, the equation <math>e^x=2</math>).{{r|oeis|berndt}}

===Recurrence and modular periodicity===
As well as the formulae above, the ordered Bell numbers may be calculated by the [[recurrence relation]]{{r|gross|pip}}
:<math>a(n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{n}{i}a(n-i).</math>
The intuitive meaning of this formula is that a weak ordering on <math>n</math> items may be broken down into a choice of some nonempty set of <math>i</math> items that go into the first equivalence class of the ordering, together with a smaller weak ordering on the remaining <math>n-i</math> items. There are <math>\tbinom{n}{i}</math> choices of the first set, and <math>a(n-i)</math> choices of the weak ordering on the rest of the elements. Multiplying these two factors, and then summing over the choices of how many elements to include in the first set, gives the number of weak orderings, <math>a(n)</math>. As a base case for the recurrence, <math>a(0)=1</math> (there is one weak ordering on zero items). Based on this recurrence, these numbers can be shown to obey certain periodic patterns in [[modular arithmetic]]: for sufficiently large <math>n</math>,
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>a(n+4) \equiv a(n) \pmod{10},</math>{{r|gross}}}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>a(n+20) \equiv a(n) \pmod{100},</math>}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>a(n+100) \equiv a(n) \pmod{1000},</math> and}}
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>a(n+500) \equiv a(n) \pmod{10000}.</math>{{r|kaufmann}}}}
Many more modular identities are known, including identities modulo any [[prime power]].{{r|good|poonen|diagana-maiga}} Peter Bala has conjectured that this sequence is eventually periodic (after a finite number of terms) modulo each positive integer <math>k</math>, with a period that divides [[Euler's totient function]] of <math>k</math>, the number of residues mod <math>k</math> that are relatively prime to <math>k</math>.{{r|oeis}}

==Applications==
===Combinatorial enumeration===
As has already been mentioned, the ordered Bell numbers count weak orderings, [[permutohedron]] faces, Cayley trees, Cayley permutations, and equivalent formulae in Fubini's theorem. Weak orderings in turn have many other applications. For instance, in [[horse racing]], [[photo finish]]es have eliminated most but not all ties, called in this context [[List of dead heat horse races|dead heats]], and the outcome of a race that may contain ties (including all the horses, not just the first three finishers) may be described using a weak ordering. For this reason, the ordered Bell numbers count the possible number of outcomes of a horse race.{{r|horse}} In contrast, when items are ordered or ranked in a way that does not allow ties (such as occurs with the ordering of cards in a deck of cards, or batting orders among [[baseball]] players), the number of orderings for <math>n</math> items is a [[factorial|factorial number]] <math>n!</math>,{{r|hhm}} which is significantly smaller than the corresponding ordered Bell number.{{r|ek}}

Problems in many areas can be formulated using weak orderings, with solutions counted using ordered Bell numbers. {{harvtxt|Velleman|Call|1995}} consider [[combination lock]]s with a numeric keypad, in which several keys may be pressed simultaneously and a combination consists of a sequence of keypresses that includes each key exactly once. As they show, the number of different combinations in such a system is given by the ordered Bell numbers.{{r|vc95}} In ''seru'', a Japanese technique for balancing [[assembly line]]s, cross-trained workers are allocated to groups of workers at different stages of a production line. The number of alternative assignments for a given number of workers, taking into account the choices of how many stages to use and how to assign workers to each stage, is an ordered Bell number.{{r|seru}} As another example, in the computer simulation of [[origami]], the ordered Bell numbers give the number of orderings in which the creases of a [[crease pattern]] can be folded, allowing sets of creases to be folded simultaneously.{{r|zhufil}}

In [[number theory]], an ordered [[multiplicative partition]] of a [[positive integer]] is a representation of the number as a product of one or more of its [[divisor]]s. For instance, 30 has 13 multiplicative partitions, as a product of one divisor (30 itself), two divisors (for instance {{nowrap|6 &middot; 5}}), or three divisors ({{nowrap|3 &middot; 5 &middot; 2}}, etc.). An integer is [[squarefree]] when it is a product of distinct [[prime number]]s; 30 is squarefree, but 20 is not, because its prime factorization {{nowrap|2 &middot; 2 &middot; 5}} repeats the prime 2. For squarefree numbers with <math>n</math> prime factors, an ordered multiplicative partition can be described by a weak ordering on its prime factors, describing which prime appears in which term of the partition. Thus, the number of ordered multiplicative partitions is given by <math>a(n)</math>. On the other hand, for a [[prime power]] with exponent <math>n</math>, an ordered multiplicative partition is a product of powers of the same prime number, with exponents summing to <math>n</math>, and this ordered sum of exponents is a [[composition (combinatorics)|composition]] of <math>n</math>. Thus, in this case, there are <math>2^{n-1}</math> ordered multiplicative partitions. Numbers that are neither squarefree nor prime powers have a number of ordered multiplicative partitions that (as a function of the number of prime factors) is between these two extreme cases.{{r|factorization}}

A [[parking function]], in mathematics, is a finite sequence of positive integers with the property that, for every <math>i</math> up to the sequence length, the sequence contains at least <math>i</math> values that are at most <math>i</math>. A sequence of this type, of length <math>n</math>, describes the following process: a sequence of <math>n</math> cars arrives on a street with <math>n</math> parking spots. Each car has a preferred parking spot, given by its value in the sequence. When a car arrives on the street, it parks in its preferred spot, or, if that is full, in the next available spot. A sequence of preferences forms a parking function if and only if each car can find a parking spot on or after its preferred spot. The number of parking functions of length <math>n</math> is exactly <math>(n+1)^{n-1}</math>. For a restricted class of parking functions, in which each car parks either on its preferred spot or on the next spot, the number of parking functions is given by the ordered Bell numbers. Each restricted parking function corresponds to a weak ordering in which the cars that get their preferred spot are ordered by these spots, and each remaining car is tied with the car in its preferred spot. The [[permutation]]s, counted by the factorials, are parking functions for which each car parks on its preferred spot.{{r|parking}} This application also provides a [[combinatorial proof]] for [[upper and lower bounds]] on the ordered Bell numbers of a simple form,
<math display=block>n!\le a(n) \le (n+1)^{n-1}.</math>

[[File:Tetrahedral reflection domains.png|thumb|The Coxeter complex for <math>A_3</math> cuts space into 24 triangular cones, shown here by their intersections with a [[unit sphere]]. The reflection planes of <math>A_3</math> cut the sphere in [[great circle]]s. The faces of the complex intersect the sphere in 24 triangles, 36 arcs, and 14 vertices; one more face, at the center of the sphere, is not visible.]] 
The ordered Bell number <math>a(n)</math> counts the number of faces in the [[Coxeter complex]] associated with a [[Coxeter group]] of type <math>A_{n-1}</math>. Here, a Coxeter group can be thought of as a finite system of reflection symmetries, closed under repeated reflections, whose mirrors partition a [[Euclidean space]] into the cells of the Coxeter complex. For instance, <math>a(3)=13</math> corresponds to <math>A_2</math>, the system of reflections of the [[Euclidean plane]] across three lines that meet at the origin at <math>60^\circ</math> angles. The complex formed by these three lines has 13 faces: the origin, six rays from the origin, and six regions between pairs of rays.{{r|oeis}}

{{harvtxt|Kemeny|1956}} uses the ordered Bell numbers to analyze [[Finitary relation|{{mvar|n}}-ary relation]]s, mathematical statements that might be true of some choices of the <math>n</math> arguments to the relation and false for others. He defines the "complexity" of a relation to mean the number of other relations one can derive from the given one by permuting and repeating its arguments. For instance, for <math>n=2</math>, a relation on two arguments <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> might take the form <math>y=f(x)</math>. By Kemeny's analysis, it has <math>a(n)=3</math> derived relations. These are the given relation <math>y=f(x)</math>, the [[converse relation]] <math>x=f(y)</math> obtained by swapping the arguments, and the [[unary relation]] <math>x=f(x)</math> obtained by repeating an argument. (Repeating the other argument produces the same relation.){{r|kemeny}}

{{harvtxt|Ellison|Klein|2001}} apply these numbers to [[optimality theory]] in [[linguistics]]. In this theory, grammars for [[natural language]]s are constructed by ranking certain constraints, and (in a phenomenon called factorial typology) the number of different grammars that can be formed in this way is limited to the number of permutations of the constraints. A paper reviewed by Ellison and Klein suggested an extension of this linguistic model in which ties between constraints are allowed, so that the ranking of constraints becomes a weak order rather than a total order. As they point out, the much larger magnitude of the ordered Bell numbers, relative to the corresponding [[factorial]]s, allows this theory to generate a much richer set of grammars.{{r|ek}}

===Other===
If a fair coin (with equal probability of heads or tails) is flipped repeatedly until the first time the result is heads, the number of tails follows a [[geometric distribution]]. The [[Moment (mathematics)|moments]] of this distribution are the ordered Bell numbers.{{r|oeis}}

Although the [[ordinary generating function]] of the ordered Bell numbers fails to converge, it describes a [[power series]] that (evaluated at <math>\tfrac1n</math> and then multiplied by <math>\tfrac2n</math>) provides an [[asymptotic expansion]] for the [[resistance distance]] of opposite vertices of an <math>n</math>-dimensional [[hypercube graph]]. Truncating this series to a bounded number of terms and then applying the result for unbounded values of <math>n</math> approximates the resistance to arbitrarily high order.{{r|pip}}

In the algebra of [[noncommutative ring]]s, an analogous construction to the (commutative) [[quasisymmetric function]]s produces a [[graded algebra]] WQSym whose dimensions in each grade are given by the ordered Bell numbers.{{r|trialgebras|feray}}

In [[spam filtering]], the problem of assigning weights to sequences of words with the property that the weight of any sequence exceeds the sum of weights of all its subsequences can be solved by using weight <math>W(n)</math> for a sequence of <math>n</math> words, where <math>W(n)</math> is obtained from the [[recurrence equation]]
<math display=block>W(n)=1+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\binom{n}{k}W(n-1),</math>
with base case <math>W(1)=0</math>. This recurrence differs from the one given earlier for the ordered Bell numbers, in two respects: omitting the <math>W(0)</math> term from the sum (because only nonempty sequences are considered), and adding one separately from the sum (to make the result exceed, rather than equalling, the sum). These differences have offsetting effects, and the resulting weights are the ordered Bell numbers.{{r|spam}}
